issues.description: The manuscript uses a 'randomized dataset' for the results and participant sections. While noted as a placeholder for pre-registration, a scientific review cannot evaluate the validity of findings or the robustness of the conclusions when the data presented is simulated and not the actual experimental results.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection.

issues.description: The manuscript identifies the design as 'within-subject,' but the procedures and the ANOVA structure (2x3) describe a between-subjects design where participants are assigned to specific conditions. If it were truly within-subjects, every participant would experience all six conditions, which is not the case here.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.description: The text states that participants 'selected their preferred' conditions. In an experimental design, random assignment is required to establish causality. Allowing participants to choose their condition introduces massive selection bias and invalidates the experimental manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The original study used real monetary stakes ($5 bills given to participants). The replication uses 'imaginary donation.' Hypothetical bias is a well-documented phenomenon where people are more generous with imaginary money than real money, potentially invalidating the comparison to the original effect size.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The original study used Ordered Probit Regression to account for the bounded and non-normal nature of donation data (often clustered at $0 and the maximum). The replication switches to ANOVA, which assumes normality and may be inappropriate for this type of DV.
issues.quote: Table 5 compares the statistical tests adopted in the original study and replication. ... Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The results section claims the interaction effect was 'supported' (p=.015), but the subsequent contrast test (Table 11) shows no significant difference (p=.558) between the key condition (Identifiable/No Intervention) and the others. This is a contradiction in the interpretation of the interaction.
issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that ... the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported. ... This replication did not find any difference between the donation under the identifiable/no intervention condition and combination of other conditions

issues.description: The 'Identifiable Victim Effect' predicts higher donations to identifiable victims. However, the replication results (even if dummy data) show the opposite: statistical victims received more (M=2.54) than identifiable victims (M=2.24). The manuscript fails to address that this is a reversal of the theory being replicated.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: The manuscript describes an eta-squared of .04 as a 'medium' effect size. By standard conventions (Cohen), .01 is small, .06 is medium, and .14 is large. Labeling .04 as medium is an overestimation.
issues.quote: The interaction effect was d = 0.41, 95% CI [0.05, 0.77] when explicit learning was adopted to debias the identifiable victim effect. The effect sizes were all considered as medium

issues.description: Table 2 lists 'N/A' for Standard Deviations in the original study. Without SDs, the calculation of Cohen's d and the power analysis for the replication cannot be fully verified by the reader.
issues.quote: Table 2 ... Identifiable victim | 2.38 | N/A

issues.description: The study aggregates 'upset,' 'sympathy,' 'moral responsibility,' and 'donation appropriateness' into a single 'aggregated feelings' score. These represent distinct affective and cognitive constructs; combining them may mask specific effects or create a construct that lacks theoretical coherence.
issues.quote: Note: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation

issues.description: The shift from a university student center (original) to Amazon Mechanical Turk (replication) involves a significant change in population demographics and environment. MTurk workers are known to be 'professional' survey takers, which may affect the 'deliberative thinking' manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The dummy data generated for the pre-registration includes a mean age of 67.8 and a range up to 120. This is highly unrepresentative of an MTurk population and suggests the simulation parameters were not calibrated to the expected sample.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; ... Age range (years) 18-120

issues.description: Several critical links for peer review and presentation materials are left as placeholders, preventing a full evaluation of the study's transparency.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>

issues.description: The researchers conducted multiple ANOVAs on 'segregated feelings' (Table 13) without applying a correction for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni) across the different dependent variables, increasing the Type I error rate.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions

issues.description: By merging Study 1 and Study 3, the researchers introduced 'Intervention applied to the joint condition.' This deviates from the original design and may introduce a confound where the implicit effect of the joint condition is obscured by the explicit intervention.
issues.quote: Intervention applied to the joint condition To combine study 1 and 3 into a single study, intervention will be applied to the joint condition

issues.description: The manuscript refers to 'implicitly learning' about the effect. In the context of Study 3, this is not 'learning' but rather a situational prime or a joint evaluation mode. 'Learning' implies an acquisition of knowledge, which Study 3 specifically avoids to test implicit mechanisms.
issues.quote: Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim

issues.description: The manuscript mentions excluding participants with prior knowledge or those who failed attention checks but does not provide the number of participants excluded, which is necessary to evaluate the final sample's composition.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The study reports a correlation of r = -.12 and r = .14 as non-significant (p > .05) with N=1000. In a sample of 1000, even very small correlations should be significant. This suggests the dummy data generation or the calculation of p-values for the correlation table may be inconsistent.
issues.quote: Identifiable/ Intervention | -.12 | .132 ... Statistical/ Intervention | .14 | .072

issues.description: The original study gave participants $5 for a 'pre-survey' to ensure they felt the money was theirs to donate (endowment effect). The replication removes this, which may change the psychological nature of the donation from 'giving up earned money' to 'allocating windfall/hypothetical credits.'
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: Table 9 reports a significant interaction (p=.015), but the abstract states 'found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.' This is a contradiction between the reported statistics and the summary conclusion.
issues.quote: found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. ... Interaction ... Replication | 2 | 4.25 | .015*
